This book covers syllabus topics 1–3: physical quantities and units, kinematics and dynamics (AS content, examined in Papers 1, 2 and 3 and assumed in Paper 4). The data sheet in the exam gives g = 9.81 m s⁻², which we use throughout. Every calculation here was checked by computer. Mark guides are our own, in the Cambridge style: C1 = a working mark (given automatically if the final answer is correct), M1 = method, A1 = answer, B1 = independent point. They are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: SI Units and Homogeneity

Key ideas

  • SI base quantities and units: mass (kg), length (m), time (s), current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol).
  • Derived units are expressed in base units: N = kg m s⁻²; J = kg m² s⁻²; W = kg m² s⁻³; Pa = kg m⁻¹ s⁻²; C = A s; V = kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹.
  • Homogeneous equation: every term has the same base units. Homogeneity is necessary but not sufficient for correctness (numerical constants can't be checked).

Worked examples

Example 1: check v² = u² + 2as: v² → m² s⁻²; 2as → (m s⁻²)(m) = m² s⁻² ✓ homogeneous.

Example 2: base units of the Young modulus (stress/strain): Pa = N m⁻² = kg m⁻¹ s⁻².

Example 3: the drag force F = kv²: k has units N/(m² s⁻²) = kg m⁻¹.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) State the SI base units of: (i) force; (ii) power; (iii) charge. [3]

(b) The speed v of a wave on a string is given by v = √(T/μ), where T is the tension and μ is the mass per unit length. Show that the equation is homogeneous. [3]

(c) The energy E stored in a capacitor is E = ½CV². Use base units to find the base units of capacitance C. [3]

(d) Explain why a homogeneous equation might still be incorrect. [1]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) (i) kg m s⁻²; (ii) kg m² s⁻³; (iii) A s (B1 each).
  • (b) T/μ: (kg m s⁻²)/(kg m⁻¹) = m² s⁻² (C1 C1); √ gives m s⁻¹, the unit of v (A1).
  • (c) C = 2E/V²: (kg m² s⁻²)/(kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹)² (C1) = (kg m² s⁻²)/(kg² m⁴ s⁻⁶ A⁻²) (C1) = kg⁻¹ m⁻² s⁴ A² (A1).
  • (d) Numerical constants (such as ½ or 2π) have no units, so they can't be checked (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Using derived units (N, J) when base units are asked.
  2. Including the kelvin or mole where they don't belong.
  3. Squaring units incorrectly.
  4. Thinking homogeneity proves an equation is correct.
  5. Confusing the unit of mass per unit length (kg m⁻¹).

Quick recall

  1. Base units of a newton?
  2. Base units of a joule?
  3. Is temperature a base quantity?
  4. Base units of pressure?
  5. Can homogeneity check the ½ in ½mv²?

Answers: 1) kg m s⁻². 2) kg m² s⁻². 3) Yes (K). 4) kg m⁻¹ s⁻². 5) No.
